claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has enhanced plastic strain relative to commercially used pure tungsten at high temperature.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has enhanced toughness relative to commercially used pure tungsten at high temperature.
Lattice distortion-induced dislocation-core spreading governs the proposed enhancement in plastic strain and toughness.
Dislocation-core spreading promotes more homogeneous plastic deformation and delays crack initiation.
Commercially used pure tungsten is characterized by long, straight dislocation lines.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has a random atomic distribution.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has significant local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions in WTaTiVZr arise from atomic-size mismatch among W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr.
Severe lattice distortion in WTaTiVZr spreads dislocation cores.
Severe lattice distortion in WTaTiVZr induces wavy dislocation lines.
The modified dislocation behavior distributes plastic deformation and reduces localized stress accumulation.
Under testing at 700–900°C, WTaTiVZr will exhibit higher plastic strain before failure than pure tungsten.
Under testing at 700–900°C, WTaTiVZr will exhibit wavier dislocation patterns than pure tungsten.
Under testing at 700–900°C, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater toughness than pure tungsten.
Pure tungsten typically undergoes limited plastic deformation and brittle fracture under the specified high-temperature conditions.
The limited plasticity of pure tungsten under these conditions is due to unmodulated dislocation motion.
The proposed mechanism is valid in high-temperature regimes where dislocation glide is active.
Lower temperatures or secondary-phase formation may cause WTaTiVZr to deviate from the predicted behavior.
Prolonged service may produce secondary-phase segregation that influences mechanical performance.

A comparison at 700–900°C with comparable grain sizes and no secondary-phase precipitates can test the proposed association among lattice distortion, dislocation morphology, plastic strain, and toughness.
